snippet.title: Chip War: The Secret Battle for the World's Most Valuable Tech
snippet.description:
Hidden beneath daily life, a silent technological cold war is raging — and it’s about semiconductors. In "The Secret Battle for the World's Most Valuable Tech," we unpack Asia’s high-stakes Chip Wars: Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, and China vying for semiconductor supremacy. Learn why chips power AI, smartphones, and the global industry, how supply-chain shocks ripple across economies, and why national security now hinges on advanced node dominance. We explore R&D, subsidies, espionage risks, and whether one nation can prevail. Essential viewing for tech enthusiasts and students who want to understand the future of innovation and geopolitics. snippet.title: The incredible engineering of Venice - Stephanie H. Smith
snippet.description:
Explore the history of Venice to find out how the infamous floating city was built and how the republic became a hub for trade.

--

To escape Germanic invaders, people fled into the Venetian Lagoon in the 6th century. The settlers set out to tame the mudflats and built a foundation in the marshy maze to support heavier, longer-lasting structures. Little did they know, this system of wood, water, and mud would still be supporting an infamous floating city 1,500 years later. Stephanie H. Smith explores the history of Venice.

snippet.title: How a decade of underinvestment is reshaping the global hunt for oil, with APA’s Tracey Henderson
snippet.description:
Let’s Talk Energy and look at the growing resurgence in oil and gas exploration. Starting in the 20-teens, many oil companies began cutting exploration budgets and letting go or reassigning the people behind that work. The shift was driven by efficiency gains and the rise of vast US shale fields, but also pressure from investors and the uncertainty over the long-term demand for oil. Now, however, oil demand is expected to remain resilient, shale fields are showing their limits and investors are asking companies whether they are finding enough barrels to maintain their cash returns, exploration is back in vogue. But rebuilding an exploration portfolio doesn’t happen overnight and the industry as a whole is finding less oil and making fewer large discoveries than it used to each year.  

+ How has the exploration business evolved over Tracey’s career and what defines a successful wildcat today?
+ How is APA Corporation, which kept exploring when others did not, looking at its prospects in places as diverse as Suriname, Uruguay, Egypt, and the Permian?
+ Can new technology and new ideas help the industry break out of its discovery drought?

snippet.title: How Government Budgets Work | Public Finance Explained
snippet.description:
Public finance explains how governments collect revenue, prepare budgets, manage spending, and borrow money.

In this video, we explain taxes, public expenditure, budget deficits, government debt, and why financial accountability matters.

What You’ll Learn
• how governments raise money
• how public budgets are created
• why deficits and debt happen

What Is Public Finance?
Public finance covers how governments:
• collect revenue
• spend public money
• manage borrowing and debt

Its goal is to fund public services while supporting economic and social priorities.

Government Revenue
Governments mainly raise money through:
• taxes
• service fees
• income from public assets

Taxes may come from personal income, businesses, property, and purchases.

What Is a Public Budget?
A public budget is the government’s financial plan for a specific period.

It shows:
• expected revenue
• planned spending
• financial priorities

The budget determines which services and projects receive funding.

Public Expenditure
Governments spend money on areas such as:
• healthcare and education
• security and infrastructure
• welfare and public services

Spending decisions reflect political priorities and public needs.

Simple Example
Imagine a government collects £100 billion in revenue.
It must decide how much to spend on hospitals, schools, transport, policing, and welfare.
Funding one area more heavily may mean reducing spending elsewhere or borrowing additional money.

Budget Deficit and Surplus
A budget deficit happens when spending is higher than revenue.
A budget surplus happens when revenue is higher than spending.
Governments may borrow to cover deficits, but continuous borrowing increases public debt.

Why Governments Borrow
Governments may borrow to:
• build major infrastructure
• respond to emergencies
• support the economy during recessions

Borrowing can be useful, but the debt and interest must eventually be managed.

Financial Accountability
Public money should be monitored through:
• audits
• transparent reporting
• parliamentary or legal oversight

Without accountability, public finance can suffer from waste, corruption, and poor spending decisions.

Reality Check
A government budget is not simply a list of numbers.
Every spending decision creates winners, losers, and trade-offs.

The brutal truth is:
Governments cannot fund every promise without raising taxes, cutting other spending, or increasing debt.

Why This Matters
Understanding public finance explains:
• where government money comes from
• why some services receive more funding
• how debt affects future budgets

Because at the end:
Public finance is about using limited public money to meet unlimited public needs.

snippet.title: The Hormuz crisis and the real cost of a barrel of oil, with Paola Rodriguez-Masiu
snippet.description:
Let’s Talk Energy and dive into the details of the stressed physical oil market. According to the news, Brent oil is trading around $95 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate or WTI is around $88. But refiners will tell you that finding a barrel that can be delivered today at those prices is difficult, and they may need to pay as much as $15 or $20 more, challenging the economics of making gasoline, diesel and jet fuel. That difference between the financial – or paper markets – and the market for physical barrels has big implications for fuel supplies and how we think about the potential impacts of the war on the global economy.  

+ How much does it really cost to buy a barrel of oil, and how has the gap between futures and physical markets trended since the start of the war?
+ What does this mean for the refining sector and the prices consumers will pay to fill up their tank or buy a plane ticket?
+ What options do governments have left to try to limit the economic damage from the energy crisis?

snippet.title: Transaction Processing Systems in Business | Examples and Functions
snippet.description:
Every organisation processes transactions.
A transaction can be:
• a customer purchase
• a restaurant order
• a hotel booking
• a bank withdrawal
• a salary payment
• an inventory update

These routine activities must be recorded accurately.

Here’s the reality:
A Transaction Processing System collects, processes, stores, and updates the daily transactions of an organisation.
In this lecture, we explain Transaction Processing Systems, how they work, where they are used, and why they are essential for modern businesses.

What You’ll Learn
• what a Transaction Processing System is
• what counts as a business transaction
• how TPS processes daily activities
• common examples of TPS
• the difference between batch and real-time processing
• the benefits and limitations of TPS

What Is a Transaction?
A transaction is a completed business activity that changes organisational records.

Examples include:
• making a sale
• receiving a payment
• placing an order
• booking a room
• checking in for work
• withdrawing money
• updating inventory

Each transaction creates data that must be recorded.

What Is TPS?
TPS stands for Transaction Processing System.
It is an Information System designed to process large numbers of routine transactions.

Its main goals are:
• speed
• accuracy
• reliability
• consistency
• security

TPS is usually used at the operational level of an organisation.

How TPS Works
A typical TPS follows four basic steps:
1. Data Input
The system collects transaction data.
Examples include:
• product scanned
• payment entered
• booking submitted
• employee checked in

2. Processing
The system checks and processes the information.
It may:
• calculate totals
• verify payment
• check availability
• update balances
• apply discounts

3. Data Storage
The transaction is saved in a database.

4. Output
The system produces an output such as:
• receipt
• confirmation
• updated balance
• order ticket
• inventory record

Examples of TPS
Retail
• point-of-sale systems
• barcode scanning
• payment processing
• inventory updates

Banking
• cash withdrawals
• deposits
• transfers
• card payments

Restaurants
• customer orders
• kitchen tickets
• payments
• stock deductions

Hotels
• reservations
• check-ins
• room payments
• cancellations

Payroll
• employee working hours
• salary calculations
• tax deductions
• wage payments

Batch Processing
In batch processing, transactions are collected and processed together later.

Examples include:
• monthly payroll
• utility bills
• end-of-day reports
• bulk bank processing

Batch processing is useful when immediate updates are not required.

Real-Time Processing
In real-time processing, transactions are processed immediately.
Examples include:
• card payments
• ATM withdrawals
• online bookings
• stock updates
• airline reservations

Real-time systems provide instant results.

TPS vs MIS
TPS records routine transactions.
MIS uses that transaction data to create reports for managers.

In simple terms:
TPS records what happened.
MIS summarises what happened.
For example:
• TPS records every sale
• MIS creates the weekly sales report

Benefits of TPS
• processes large numbers of transactions
• reduces manual work
• improves accuracy
• provides faster service
• updates records automatically
• supports daily operations
• creates data for other systems

Limitations of TPS
• system failure can stop operations
• inaccurate input creates incorrect records
• cyberattacks can expose sensitive data
• employees may become dependent on automation
• implementation can be expensive
• TPS mainly supports routine decisions

The Real Shift
• from manual records → automated transactions
• from slow processing → instant updates
• from paper receipts → digital records
• from isolated activities → connected databases
• from human calculations → system accuracy

Reality Check
• TPS does not make strategic decisions
• it depends heavily on accurate input
• reliability is critical
• downtime can immediately affect customers
• security is essential because transaction data may be sensitive

Why This Matters
Without an effective TPS:
• sales may be recorded incorrectly
• payments may fail
• bookings may be duplicated
• inventory may become inaccurate
• customer service may slow down
• managers may receive unreliable reports

Because at the end:
Transaction Processing Systems are the operational foundation of modern organisations because they record the everyday activities on which every other business system depends.

snippet.title: How the worst oil crisis ever recorded could end in energy abundance, with Claudio Galimberti
snippet.description:
Join us for our annual Summits in Singapore, Houston and London: https://rystad.info/3SfZuBC  

Let’s Talk Energy and assess the possible long-term impacts of the war in the Middle East. The conflict has brought the geopolitics of energy and near-term market disruptions into sharp focus, as the world struggles with higher oil and natural gas prices and tighter supplies overall.  

But underlying fundamentals, which pointed to growing oversupply in both oil and, to a lesser extent, gas markets, persist despite war-driven distortions.  

And while no one can predict how long it could take for the US and Iran to reach an agreement to resolve the war, the two sides continue to negotiate and – at times – say they are making progress.

+ How long could the war-driven shortages and price inflation that we see today persist after the US and Iran reach some sort of agreement to end the conflict and fully re-open the Strait of Hormuz? 
+ What changes to energy trade flows or policies could be more lasting and what shifts might be less durable as countries and markets digest this shock and steel themselves against future ones? 
+ Which factors will be most important to watch to determine how the world ultimately recovers from a massive shock to the energy system?

snippet.title: Executive Information Systems | Dashboards, KPIs and Strategy
snippet.description:
An Executive Information System, or EIS, helps senior leaders monitor performance, identify trends, and make strategic decisions.

In this lecture, we explain how EIS uses dashboards, summaries, and key performance indicators to turn complex data into clear executive insights.

EIS helps leaders focus on risks, opportunities, and long-term business goals.

What Is an Executive Information System?

An Executive Information System is designed mainly for senior executives.

It provides quick access to important internal and external information.

Executives use it to understand:
• overall business performance
• major risks and opportunities
• market and competitor activity

Who Uses EIS?
EIS is commonly used by:
• chief executive officers
• directors and senior executives
• business owners and strategic leaders

These users are responsible for the long-term direction of the organisation.

Main Features of EIS
Dashboards
Dashboards display important information in one place.

They may include:
• revenue and profit
• customer growth
• operational performance

Key Performance Indicators
KPIs help executives measure whether the organisation is achieving its goals.

Examples include:
• profit margin
• customer retention
• market growth

Trend Analysis
EIS helps leaders identify patterns over time.
It may show whether sales, costs, demand, or performance are increasing or decreasing.

Internal and External Information
EIS combines information from inside and outside the organisation.

Internal Information
• financial performance
• sales results
• employee productivity

External Information
• market trends
• economic conditions
• competitor activity

This gives executives a broader view of the business environment.

Example of EIS
Imagine a restaurant company with several branches.
Its executive dashboard may display:
• total revenue across all branches
• the most and least profitable locations
• customer satisfaction trends
• rising food and staffing costs
• progress towards expansion goals

Executives can quickly identify where attention is needed.

EIS vs MIS
A Management Information System provides regular reports for operational and middle managers.

An Executive Information System provides summarised strategic information for senior leaders.

In simple terms:
MIS helps managers control current performance.
EIS helps executives guide the organisation’s future.

EIS vs DSS
A Decision Support System helps analyse specific complex decisions.
An Executive Information System provides a broader overview of organisational performance.

DSS explores a particular problem.
EIS monitors the bigger strategic picture.

Benefits of EIS
• quick access to critical information
• better strategic planning
• early identification of risks
• clearer performance monitoring
• improved executive decision-making

Limitations of EIS
• inaccurate data can mislead executives
• dashboards may oversimplify complex problems
• implementation can be expensive
• executives may focus on the wrong metrics
• the system cannot replace leadership judgement

The Real Shift
• from detailed reports → executive summaries
• from operational data → strategic insights
• from delayed information → real-time dashboards
• from isolated figures → organisation-wide performance
• from reacting to problems → identifying risks earlier

Reality Check
• more dashboard data does not guarantee better decisions
• important information can be hidden by poor design
• KPIs must match real business goals
• external events can make predictions unreliable
• executives remain responsible for final decisions

Why This Matters
Without effective executive information:
• leaders may miss important trends
• strategic risks may remain hidden
• departments may move in different directions
• decisions may depend on incomplete information
• organisations may react too slowly to change

Because at the end:
An Executive Information System does not give leaders every piece of data—it gives them the critical information needed to understand performance and guide the organisation’s future.

snippet.title: A Gambling Streak Invented Your Favorite Food #foodfacts #sandwich
snippet.description:

The word "sandwich" traces directly to John Montagu, the 4th Earl of Sandwich, who in the 1760s ordered meat between two slices of bread during a 24-hour gambling session so he could eat without leaving the card table. Other players copied the order by name. The term spread across England and eventually the world. Today an estimated 300 million sandwiches are consumed globally every day.

John Montagu was too addicted to gambling to eat properly so now we have sandwiches.

snippet.title: Decision Support Systems in Business | Examples and Benefits
snippet.description:
Some business decisions are simple.
Others involve risk, uncertainty, and several possible options.

A Decision Support System, or DSS, helps managers analyse data, compare alternatives, and understand possible outcomes before making a decision.

In this lecture, you will learn:
• what a Decision Support System is
• how DSS supports complex decisions
• the difference between DSS and MIS
• common examples and benefits of DSS
• why human judgement is still necessary

DSS can be used for forecasting, risk analysis, planning, and what-if scenarios.

It does not replace managers.
It gives them better information to make stronger decisions.
